Why Greece is not usually included? 
That label is not a ranking of “great civilizations,” but a textbook-style category focusing on the earliest river-valley civilizations that developed large-scale states, urban centers, and writing very early—Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus region, and China. By contrast, Greek civilization reached its major florescence later and grew in a different Mediterranean, city-state (polis) pattern shaped by maritime trade and decentralized political life rather than the classic river-valley model. In other words, Greece is foundational to Western culture, but it is typically treated as a later, distinct civilization that built on earlier Near Eastern and Egyptian developments rather than one of the earliest “cradles” in that specific framework.

For the Roman calendar, you can focus on three main stages: the early Roman calendar, the Julian calendar, and today’s Gregorian calendar. The early system was irregular—months could have shifting lengths, and officials sometimes inserted extra days or even an extra month to keep the year aligned with the seasons, which made the calendar confusing and open to manipulation. To fix this, Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar in 46 BCE, creating a more stable 365-day year with a leap day every four years. Much later, the Gregorian calendar refined the Julian system by adjusting leap-year rules to correct small long-term drift.

THE JUDGEMENT OF PARIS was a contest between the three most beautiful goddesses of Olympos--Aphrodite, Hera and Athena--for the prize of a golden apple addressed "To the Fairest."
The story began with the wedding of Peleus and Thetis which all the gods had been invited to attend except for Eris, goddess of discord. When Eris appeared at the festivities she was turned away and in her anger cast the golden apple amongst the assembled goddesses addressed "To the Fairest." Three goddesses laid claim to the apple--Aphrodite, Hera and Athena. Zeus was asked to mediate and he commanded Hermes to lead the three goddesses to Paris of Troy to decide the issue. The three goddesses appearing before the shepherd prince, each offering him gifts for favour. He chose Aphrodite, swayed by her promise to bestow upon him Helene, the most beautiful woman, for wife. The subsequent abduction of Helene (Menelaus’ wife-then) led directly to the Trojan War and the fall of the city.

Plot of Iliad: 
The Iliad tells the story of Achilles’ rage during the final year of the Trojan War. The conflict begins when Agamemnon, leader of the Greek army, takes Briseis from Achilles, dishonoring him and causing Achilles to withdraw from battle. Without their greatest warrior, the Greeks suffer heavy losses, and the Trojan prince Hector leads successful attacks against them. The turning point comes when Achilles’ close companion Patroclus enters the battle wearing Achilles’ armor but is killed by Hector. Overcome with grief and anger, Achilles returns to fight, reconciles with Agamemnon, and kills Hector in single combat, dragging his body in revenge. 

The Meaning of the name: Iliad=the song of Ilion/Troy  
In the end, Hector’s father, King Priam of Troy, bravely visits Achilles and begs for his son’s body. Moved by Priam’s sorrow, Achilles returns the body, and the epic ends with Hector’s funeral, highlighting both the tragedy of war and the shared humanity of enemies.

2.6.3 Achilles' Heel 🌟

Definition (p.19) 

A weakness in spite of overall strength, which can lead to a downfall

Achilles’ death is not narrated in Homer’s Iliad and is only indirectly referenced in the Odyssey. In later Trojan War traditions, Achilles is killed toward the end of the war—most commonly by an arrow shot by Paris, often with Apollo’s assistance. The famous detail of the “Achilles’ heel” represents a later development of the myth, turning his death into a lasting metaphor for a fatal weakness.

Odyssey: Odysseus, Ithaca
Siren's song.

The Odyssey follows Odysseus’s long journey home after the Trojan War. While his wife Penelope is pressured by arrogant 108 suitors who waste his household, Odysseus struggles to return, facing monsters, storms, and divine hostility—most notably from Poseidon for the blindness of his son Polyphemus[独眼巨人波吕斐摩斯]. After years of wandering, he finally reaches Ithaca, disguises himself, reunites with his son Telemachus, and carefully plans revenge. In the climax, Odysseus proves his identity, defeats the suitors, and restores order to his home, ending with his reunion with Penelope.

In The Odyssey, the Sirens use their enchanting voices to lure sailors to their destruction. Their song promises irresistible knowledge, glory, and understanding, tempting listeners to abandon reason and steer their ships toward the dangerous shore. Unable to resist the overwhelming desire to hear more, sailors lose control and crash upon the rocks, where death awaits them. Knowing the danger, Odysseus orders his crew to block their ears with wax and tie him to the mast so he can hear the song without acting on its temptation. The Sirens’ deception represents the powerful and often dangerous nature of temptation, showing how desire and curiosity can lead to ruin if not restrained by discipline and foresight.

The Aeneid, written by Virgil, tells the story of Aeneas, a Trojan hero and the son of Venus and Anchises, who escapes from the burning city of Troy after its fall. Guided by fate, he travels across the Mediterranean in search of a new homeland where he is destined to found the ancestors of the Roman people. Along the way, he falls in love with Queen Dido of Carthage but leaves her to fulfill his divine mission, causing her tragic death. Aeneas later journeys to the underworld, where he learns about Rome’s future greatness. Eventually, he reaches Italy and fights a war against local forces led by Turnus. The epic ends with Aeneas defeating Turnus, securing his destiny and laying the foundation for the future rise of Rome.
Carthage /ˈkɑːrθɪdʒ/ —— 迦太基

Carthage was a Phoenician city-state on the coast of North Africa (the site of modern-day Tunis) which, prior the conflict with Rome known as the Punic Wars (264-146 BCE), was the largest, most affluent, and powerful political entity in the Mediterranean.

In The Aeneid (Book 2), Aeneas recounts the night Troy fell. The Greeks pretend to sail away, leaving behind the Trojan Horse, and a Greek captive, Sinon, deceives the Trojans into bringing it inside the city despite warnings. That night Greek warriors emerge from the horse, open the gates, and the Greek army floods in, destroying Troy. Aeneas briefly fights back, but Hector’s ghost and Venus reveal that Troy’s fall is fated, and he must escape to fulfill his destiny. He flees the burning city carrying his aged father Anchises and leading his son, while losing his wife Creusa in the chaos, and thus Troy’s ruin becomes the beginning of Aeneas’s mission to found a new homeland in Italy.
